lessons.title: Corporate Earnings and Margins: How They Move With the Cycle

body.text: Corporate earnings don't just follow GDP, they amplify it. A modest swing in revenue growth can produce a much larger swing in profit, and that amplification is the biggest reason equity markets move more violently than the economy they're pricing.

children.text: The first two lessons of this chapter showed which sectors, styles, and sizes lead at different points in the cycle. This lesson explains the mechanism sitting underneath all of that: why corporate earnings, the thing every one of those rotations is ultimately about, swing so much harder than the GDP growth rate that drives them.
Operating Leverage: Why Profits Swing Harder Than Revenue

markDefs.definition: The degree to which a company's profit changes for a given change in revenue, driven by how much of its cost base is fixed (rent, salaries, depreciation) versus variable (raw materials, sales commissions). Higher fixed costs mean higher operating leverage.

children.text: Most companies carry two kinds of costs: fixed costs, like factory rent, plant depreciation, and a base level of staff, that stay roughly the same whatever the revenue is, and variable costs, like raw materials, that move directly with revenue. This split creates
: once fixed costs are covered, almost every extra rupee of revenue drops straight to profit, and the reverse is just as painful when revenue falls.

body.caption: Variable costs move with revenue; fixed costs don't, which is exactly what creates the leverage
A company with ₹600 crore fixed costs and variable costs at 30% of revenue

body.text: A 10% move in revenue, in either direction, produces a 70% move in profit here. That 7-to-1 ratio is the degree of operating leverage, and it is far higher for capital-intensive, fixed-cost-heavy businesses like cement, steel, and airlines than for asset-light businesses like IT services or FMCG distribution. This is a large part of why cyclical sectors, the ones flagged in Lesson 1, see such extreme earnings and share price swings across the cycle.

body.title: Compare a Less Fixed-Cost-Heavy Business
body.prompt: A different company has ₹1,000 crore revenue, ₹400 crore fixed costs, and variable costs at 40% of revenue. If revenue rises 10%, by what percentage does profit change? Enter a positive number.
body.explanation: Base profit = 1,000 − 400 − 400 = ₹200 cr. At 10% higher revenue: 1,100 − 400 − 440 = ₹260 cr, a 30% increase. This company's degree of operating leverage is 3-to-1, far lower than the 7-to-1 example above, because a smaller share of its costs are fixed. Lower fixed-cost businesses have gentler earnings swings across the cycle, in both directions.

body.caption: What margins are typically doing in each phase

cells: Volumes rise, fixed costs spread over more revenue, operating leverage works in the company's favour
Input costs and wages start rising, eating into the operating leverage tailwind
Volumes fall while fixed costs stay put, operating leverage works against the company
Cost-cutting takes hold and sets an unusually low base, which flatters the next expansion's growth rate

children.text: Why Nifty Earnings Grew Even When GDP Didn't: Two Structural Boosts

Not every margin improvement is cyclical. Two genuinely structural changes boosted Nifty earnings over the last several years, independent of where the demand cycle stood, and it matters that you can tell them apart from ordinary operating leverage.

stats.context: Effective rate for existing domestic companies, including surcharge and cess

stats.label: Corporate tax rate, after the cut
stats.context: For companies opting into the new lower-rate regime, effective from FY20

stats.label: Bank gross NPA ratio, FY18
stats.context: Peak stressed-asset ratio for scheduled commercial banks

stats.label: Bank gross NPA ratio, FY24
stats.context: Multi-year cleanup meant sharply lower provisioning, a direct boost to bank profits

body.text: The September 2019 corporate tax cut and the multi-year cleanup in bank bad loans both show up in the same place, Nifty EPS growth, as ordinary operating leverage does. But they are not the same thing. Operating leverage on rising volumes is cyclical and tends to reverse when volumes fall. A one-time tax rate cut and a completed NPA cleanup are structural, they don't mechanically reverse just because the cycle turns down again. Knowing which kind of margin expansion you're looking at changes how durable you should expect the resulting earnings growth to be.

body.title: Cyclical or Structural?
body.scenario: A cement company's operating margin has expanded from 18% to 24% over two years. Management credits it to "higher capacity utilisation and better cost control." Separately, a private bank's net profit has grown strongly for three years, driven mainly by a steadily falling provisioning charge as its old bad-loan book has been resolved.
body.prompt: Which of these two margin expansions is more cyclical, and which is more structural? What would make you cautious about extrapolating either one in a valuation?
body.modelAnswer: The cement company's margin expansion is largely cyclical: it is explicitly tied to capacity utilisation, which is operating leverage on rising volumes, and it should be expected to compress again once volumes soften or new capacity comes online. The bank's margin expansion is closer to structural: once a bad-loan book is fully resolved, provisioning charges naturally normalise lower and don't automatically shoot back up unless a fresh credit cycle turns bad. The caution in both cases is the same: it is tempting to draw a straight line through recent margin trends into a valuation model, but the cement company's margins should be modelled as mean-reverting with the cycle, while the bank's lower provisioning is a more durable new normal, unless a new round of credit stress begins.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: A company's revenue growth has decelerated for two quarters, but its operating margin is still near a multi-year high and management just announced a large capacity expansion. Which phase does this best describe?
body.explanation: Decelerating growth combined with still-high margins is the hallmark of a peak: the good times haven't shown up as a problem in the margin line yet, but the deceleration and the aggressive capacity expansion, which will add fixed costs just as growth is slowing, are both classic late-cycle signals.

body.text: The most common way investors get hurt by operating leverage is paying a growth-stock valuation, discussed in the last lesson, for earnings that are actually cyclical margins near their peak. If a company's margin is well above its 10-year average and its growth is decelerating, that is exactly the combination the framework says to treat with the most caution, not the most enthusiasm.

cards.definition: The degree to which profit changes for a given change in revenue, driven by the fixed-versus-variable split in a company's cost base.
Costs that stay roughly the same regardless of revenue, such as rent, depreciation, and base staffing.
Costs that move directly with revenue, such as raw materials and sales commissions.
Margin improvement driven by rising volumes and operating leverage, which tends to reverse when volumes fall.
Margin improvement from a durable, one-time change such as a tax rate cut or a completed bad-loan cleanup, which does not mechanically reverse with the cycle.

body.text: Cost structures, tax rates, and NPA figures in this lesson are simplified or rounded for teaching purposes and are provided for education only. Actual company cost structures and applicable tax provisions are more complex and vary by company and financial year. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser or a qualified tax professional for advice on your own situation.

points: Operating leverage means profit swings harder than revenue in both directions, because fixed costs don't move while variable costs do; a 10% revenue swing produced a 70% profit swing in this lesson's example
Businesses with heavier fixed costs (cement, steel, airlines) have higher operating leverage and more extreme earnings cycles than asset-light businesses (IT services, FMCG distribution)
Margins expand through expansion and peak as operating leverage works in a company's favour, then compress sharply in contraction as it works against them
Not all margin expansion is cyclical: the September 2019 corporate tax cut and the multi-year bank NPA cleanup were structural boosts to Nifty earnings, independent of the demand cycle
Telling cyclical margin expansion (which mean-reverts) apart from structural margin expansion (which mostly doesn't) changes how much of it you should extrapolate into a valuation
The riskiest combination is a growth-stock valuation paid for cyclical margins that are already near a multi-year peak with decelerating growth
